name: glommio (io_uring thread-per-core runtime)
baseline: Tokio 1.14 multi-threaded runtime with one worker per core (current_thread at 1 core), serving the same TCP ping-pong server
verdict_reason: In monoio's independent 2021 benchmark, glommio's peak QPS beat Tokio's by 1.4x at 4 cores and 2.3x at 16 cores, but it was 20% slower at 1 core and stayed behind monoio. Glommio itself publishes no runtime benchmark, and the repository has had no commit since April 2025.
tier_reason: Public third-party benchmark code and raw results with CPU, NIC, kernel and toolchain stated.
claimed_speedup: Best QPS, 100-byte ping-pong in monoio's benchmark, glommio vs Tokio: 16 cores 2064589 vs 908179, 4 cores 616687 vs 430921, 1 core 163709 vs 205726 (2.3x, 1.4x and 0.80x, derived from page data). Glommio's announcement cites outside research that thread-per-core 'can improve tail latencies of applications by up to 71%'.
workload: TCP ping-pong echo server, 100-byte messages, client machines driving a fixed number of connections per core; best QPS across connection counts.
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 5118 @ 2.30GHz server, Intel X710 10GbE NIC
one_liner: Datadog's thread-per-core io_uring runtime; 1.4-2.3x Tokio's peak QPS at 4-16 cores in a third-party 2021 echo benchmark, slower on one core.
how_it_is_fast: One executor per pinned core with its own io_uring rings (separate rings for latency-sensitive and regular I/O), so there is no cross-thread task migration or shared queue. Task queues get CPU shares, and latency-sensitive queues can preempt throughput work by polling the latency ring.
use_it_when: Sharded storage or data-plane services on Linux with many cores
Workloads that need per-queue latency classes and shares
skip_it_when: Single-core or few-connection services, where Tokio was faster in this test
Projects that need an actively maintained runtime: no commits since 2025-04-21
caveats: The only numbers come from a competitor's (monoio's) benchmark, using glommio 0.6.0 and Tokio 1.14 from 2021.
The 71% tail-latency figure in glommio's announcement is from outside research on thread-per-core designs, not a glommio measurement.
One workload (echo) on one server model.
tradeoffs: Tasks are pinned to cores; uneven load cannot be rebalanced.
Own I/O types; the Tokio ecosystem needs adapters.

evidence.quote: Glommio and the model are the same as Monoio, so it also has good horizontal scalability, but its peak performance is still a certain gap compared to Monoio.
Research recently demonstrated that a thread-per-core architecture can improve tail latencies of applications by up to 71%
The minimum version at this time is 5.8.
